items.title: Level 4: Who does what in the checks
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls; UK Security Vetting guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Several different people and teams play a part in getting you from offer to start date, and knowing their roles helps you ask the right person. The recruiting manager chooses the candidate and decides what the job needs, including the level of clearance. The department's HR or recruitment team issues the conditional offer and usually runs the baseline checks, collecting your documents and sending the forms. The security team in the department, led by a senior person often called the Departmental Security Officer, sets the department's security rules and acts as the link to the vetting organisation. For clearance above the baseline, United Kingdom Security Vetting, or UKSV, carries out the investigation. UKSV gathers information and assesses risk, but it does so on behalf of the sponsoring department, which remains responsible for deciding on the post and for managing the clearance once it is granted. You, as the candidate, have duties too. You must give full and honest information, reply promptly and report changes. Your referees and former employers are asked to confirm facts, but they do not make decisions. When you have a question, the usual route is to start with the person who sent you the request, usually HR or the security contact in the advert. They know your case and can pass the question on. Asking the vetting organisation directly is often not possible, because the department is the sponsor.

questions.prompt: Who decides what level of clearance a job needs?

options.text: The referees, based on how well they know the candidate
The recruiting department, based on the sensitivity of the work
The vetting organisation, based on the candidate's background and history
The candidate, based on the career they want to follow

questions.hint: The department sets the level in advance according to the job.

questions.prompt: Who usually issues the conditional offer and runs the baseline checks?

options.text: The department's HR or recruitment team
The vetting organisation, UKSV
The candidate's referees
The Home Office on behalf of the department

questions.hint: HR or recruitment teams usually manage the offer and baseline checks.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the department's security team?

options.text: Setting security rules and acting as the link to the vetting organisation
Providing training on writing skills for new staff
Interviewing candidates and choosing who is appointed
Running payroll and pension arrangements for new starters and leavers

questions.hint: The security team sets the rules and links the department to vetting.

questions.prompt: What does UKSV do for clearance above the baseline?

options.text: Decides which jobs are advertised in the department and what they pay
Provides the baseline checks for every new starter
Sets the salary band for cleared posts in the department
Carries out the investigation and assesses risk for the sponsoring department

questions.hint: UKSV investigates on behalf of the sponsor.

questions.prompt: Who remains responsible for managing the clearance once it is granted?

options.text: The sponsoring department
The candidate's referees
UKSV alone
The candidate's previous employer

questions.hint: The sponsor is responsible for the post and the clearance.

questions.prompt: What are the duties of the candidate during the checks?

options.text: Decide when the vetting organisation should finish its work
Contact referees and former employers to arrange the references
Give full and honest information, reply promptly and report changes
Choose the level of checks and which questions to answer

questions.hint: Candidates must be honest, prompt and report changes.

questions.prompt: What do referees and former employers do in the process?

options.text: Choose the date on which the candidate starts
Confirm facts, but they do not make decisions
Set the conditions of the job offer
Decide whether clearance is granted

questions.hint: They confirm information only.

questions.prompt: Why is it usually best to ask the person who sent you the request?

options.text: Other teams are not allowed to answer questions
They can change the outcome of the vetting
Only they are allowed to talk to the vetting organisation
They know your case and can pass the question on

questions.hint: The person who contacted you is the natural first point of contact.

items.title: Level 4: When an offer can be withdrawn
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: A conditional offer is a promise to employ you if certain conditions are met. If the conditions are not met, the department can withdraw the offer. The most common reasons are that a required document cannot be provided, that identity or the right to work cannot be confirmed, that the checks reveal information that was not declared, or that the answers on the form turn out to be untrue. A department may also withdraw an offer if a reference reveals a serious concern or if a clearance required for the role is refused. The reason matters. Missing paperwork can often be fixed by producing the document later, and a department will normally give you a reasonable time to do so. A real difficulty that you declared honestly is treated very differently from one that you hid. Departments are expected to be fair. This means they should explain what the problem is, give you a chance to respond where appropriate, and follow their own procedures. They must also follow the law, including equality law, so decisions should relate to the requirements of the role and not to protected characteristics such as race, disability or religion. If you believe a decision was unfair, you can ask for it to be looked at again, using the department's process, and you can seek advice from an independent organisation. Whatever the outcome, being honest from the start keeps your options open.

questions.prompt: What is a conditional offer?

options.text: A promise to employ you if certain conditions are met
A provisional interview slot before the offer is made
A final contract that cannot be changed once it is accepted
A guarantee of a permanent post after probation

questions.hint: The offer depends on conditions such as passing the checks.

questions.prompt: Which is a common reason for withdrawing an offer?

options.text: The candidate lives far from the office
The candidate asks a question about the contract
Answers on the form turn out to be untrue
The candidate takes a few days to reply to the offer

questions.hint: Untrue answers are a typical reason.

questions.prompt: How is missing paperwork usually treated?

options.text: It can often be fixed by producing the document later
It is replaced by a statement from a referee
It leads to automatic withdrawal of the offer in every case
It is ignored once the candidate has started

questions.hint: Departments normally allow reasonable time for paperwork.

questions.prompt: Why does it matter whether a difficulty was declared or hidden?

options.text: A declared difficulty is treated differently from one that was hidden
Both are treated in exactly the same way whatever the circumstances are
Hidden difficulties are accepted as long as they are small ones
Declared difficulties are treated more strictly than hidden ones

questions.hint: Honesty counts strongly in the department's judgement.

questions.prompt: What should a fair department do when there is a problem?

options.text: Explain it, give a chance to respond and follow its procedures
Ask the candidate to withdraw to avoid a formal decision
Pass the problem to the candidate's former employer
Withdraw the offer without any explanation in order to save time

questions.hint: Fair process includes explanation and a chance to respond.

questions.prompt: Which kind of reason would be contrary to equality law?

options.text: Withdrawing an offer because a required document was not provided in time
Withdrawing an offer because clearance for the role was refused
Withdrawing an offer because of a protected characteristic such as race
Withdrawing an offer because the right to work could not be confirmed

questions.hint: Decisions must relate to the role, not protected characteristics.

questions.prompt: What can you do if you think a decision was unfair?

options.text: Contact the vetting organisation and ask it to overturn the decision
Ask for it to be looked at again using the department's process
Start work anyway while you wait for the decision to be changed
Ask your referees to appeal to the department for you

questions.hint: Departments have a process for review.

questions.prompt: What keeps your options open whatever the outcome?

options.text: Being honest from the start
Providing as little information as possible
Replying only when asked a second time
Waiting for the department to ask about problems

questions.hint: Honesty protects your position.

items.title: Level 4: How identity is verified
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Verifying identity is more than looking at one document. The aim is to be confident that the person is real, that they are who they say they are and that they are the person in front of the checker. Several kinds of evidence help. Some documents come from official sources, such as a passport or photocard driving licence, and they usually carry a photograph. Others come from the financial or utility world and show a link to an address. The checker looks for consistency: the name, date of birth and address should match across documents, with differences explained. A checker also looks at how long and in what way the person has existed in records. A history of activity, for example in banking or employment, is harder to fake than a single document. For this reason you may be asked for more than one type of document, and the department may ask extra questions if something does not fit. Identity checks may also look at whether the document has security features, and some departments use technology to read these. If you have unusual circumstances, such as being a refugee or having no fixed address, tell the team early. Alternative evidence can often be accepted, and the team will advise. Remember that these checks protect you as well. They make it harder for another person to use your identity.

questions.prompt: What is the aim of verifying identity?

options.text: To record the person's qualifications and training to date
To be confident the person is real, is who they say and is present
To collect as many documents as possible for the personnel file
To decide which pay band the person will be placed in

questions.hint: Identity verification confirms existence and match.

questions.prompt: What do checkers look for across your documents?

options.text: That each document has the same colour of ink
That each document was issued in the same year
Consistency of name, date of birth and address
That all documents come from the same organisation

questions.hint: Consistency, with differences explained, is the key.

questions.prompt: Why is a history of activity in records useful to a checker?

options.text: It proves the person has never been in debt
It replaces the need to see any original document
It shows the person's level of income
It is harder to fake than a single document

questions.hint: A long record of activity is difficult to forge.

questions.prompt: Why might you be asked for more than one type of document?

options.text: Each department has a target number of documents to collect
Several types of evidence give greater confidence than one
One document cannot be accepted for legal reasons
The checker is paid according to the number checked

questions.hint: Multiple sources strengthen confidence.

questions.prompt: What kind of features might a checker examine on a document?

options.text: The age of the person who handed it in at the desk
Security features designed to show it is genuine
The number of times it has been photocopied
The place where the document was kept

questions.hint: Genuine documents carry security features.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible step if you have unusual circumstances, such as no fixed address?

options.text: Tell the team early so alternative evidence can be agreed
Wait to see if the checker raises it
Use the address of a friend without telling anyone at the department
Choose a different job that has no identity check

questions.hint: Alternative evidence can often be accepted if you explain early.

questions.prompt: How do identity checks protect you?

options.text: They prevent your employer from asking for more documents
They guarantee that you will be promoted
They remove the need to show your pass at work
They make it harder for someone else to use your identity

questions.hint: Strong checks protect the real person.

questions.prompt: What happens if a detail does not fit across your documents?

options.text: The department chooses which document to believe
The department accepts it without comment
The department may ask extra questions
The department rejects the application at once

questions.hint: Differences invite further questions.

items.title: Level 4: References and employment confirmation
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Employment history is confirmed in several ways. The department may ask previous employers to confirm your dates and job title, ask referees to give their view, and look at documents such as payslips, a P45 or a letter from the employer. The BPSS is mainly about verifying facts, not judging quality. A reference at this stage confirms that you worked where you said and, in some departments, whether there were any serious concerns about conduct. It is separate from the reference a recruiter may take to judge your suitability for the job. Some employers will confirm only the bare facts, such as dates and job title, because of their own policies. That is acceptable. If a previous employer cannot be traced or has closed, the department looks for other ways to confirm, such as tax records, payslips or a person who knew your work. Referees should know you in the context in which you are being verified. A friend can sometimes be accepted for a personal reference but should not be a close relative if a more independent person is available. Always ask someone before naming them, and tell them what to expect, so that they answer promptly. Giving a name of someone who does not know you is a form of dishonesty. Make sure the contact details are correct and that the referee can be reached during the checks period.

questions.prompt: What does a reference at the pre-employment stage mainly do?

options.text: Decides your pay and grade in the new role you will take up soon
Ranks you against the other candidates for the same job
Tests your skills for the tasks you will do in the post
Confirms you worked where you said, plus any serious conduct concerns

questions.hint: The BPSS reference is mainly about verifying facts.

questions.prompt: Why might some employers confirm only dates and job title?

options.text: Their own policies limit what they release
They have no records of former staff
They have to ask permission from the Home Office first
They are not allowed to speak to government departments

questions.hint: Employer policies vary, and bare facts are acceptable.

questions.prompt: How can the department confirm your history if a former employer has closed?

options.text: By accepting your own written statement without any evidence
Through payslips, tax records or a person who knew your work
By removing that period from the check without comment
By asking the Companies Registry to give a reference

questions.hint: Other evidence can be used when an employer cannot be traced.

questions.prompt: Which person would make a good referee for the employment check?

options.text: A relative who has known you well for many years
Anyone who is willing to say positive things about you in writing
Someone who knows you in the setting being verified and can be reached
A person who has not met you but has seen your CV

questions.hint: Referees should really know you in the relevant context.

questions.prompt: What is sensible before naming a referee?

options.text: Ask them first and tell them what to expect
Add them to the form to surprise them
Pick the most senior person you can find
Choose someone whose contact details you are unsure of

questions.hint: Asking first means they answer promptly.

questions.prompt: Why is naming someone who does not know you a problem?

options.text: It slows down the check but is otherwise harmless
It is allowed if the department already knows the person
It is a form of dishonesty that can end the process
It is only a problem for senior roles

questions.hint: False referees are dishonest.

questions.prompt: What other documents may support your employment history?

options.text: Your medical records and prescriptions
Payslips, a P45 or a letter from the employer
Your school reports and exam results from many years ago
Your travel tickets and hotel bookings

questions.hint: These show that you worked for the employer.

questions.prompt: What should you make sure about each referee's details?

options.text: That the referee has worked for the department before and knows the team
That the referee lives in the same town as you do, for convenience
That they are correct and the referee can be reached during checks
That the referee has a work email address only

questions.hint: Reachable, correct details avoid delays.

items.title: Level 4: Convictions, cautions and exceptions
items.body: The law on convictions that become spent is set out in the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 and later changes, and the detail differs in different parts of the UK. The principle is that if someone has stayed out of trouble for a set period, they should not be held back by an old offence. The period depends on the sentence given. Some very serious sentences never become spent. For ordinary posts, an employer cannot ask about or take into account a spent conviction, and a candidate may answer no if asked about it. Some roles are excepted from these rules. They include certain jobs in policing, the legal system, and work with children or vulnerable adults, and they may ask about spent convictions as well, although some old and minor matters may be filtered out. Cautions and some other outcomes may also have periods before they are spent. For the BPSS, the department asks about unspent convictions. It then considers the facts. It will look at how serious the matter was, how long ago it was, the person's age at the time, any pattern, and how relevant it is to the post. It may decide that the matter does not stop the appointment. The most damaging thing is to give a false answer to a question that the department is entitled to ask. If the post is an excepted one, the advert should say so.

questions.prompt: What is the main principle behind spent convictions?

options.text: Only convictions for driving offences can be spent
Someone who stays out of trouble should not be held back by an old offence
Convictions should be kept secret from the courts
Every conviction should be reported to every future employer for life

questions.hint: Rehabilitation is the idea behind the law.

questions.prompt: What does the length of the period before a conviction is spent depend on?

options.text: The sentence given
The age of the employer
The job the person applies for
The size of the fine paid

questions.hint: The sentence determines the period.

questions.prompt: Can very serious sentences become spent?

options.text: Only if the person changes name
Some never do
All do after ten years
All do after twenty years

questions.hint: Some very serious sentences never become spent.

questions.prompt: In an ordinary post, how should a spent conviction be treated?

options.text: The employer must record it on the personnel file for later
The employer must tell the person's colleagues
The employer can ask about it and decide freely what to do
The employer cannot ask about or take it into account

questions.hint: Spent convictions are protected in ordinary posts.

questions.prompt: Which type of post might be excepted from the usual rules on spent convictions?

options.text: Jobs that involve a long commute or travel abroad
Jobs in any large company that handles customer money
Jobs paid above a certain salary level in the Civil Service
Some jobs in policing, the legal system or with vulnerable people

questions.hint: Excepted posts exist for sensitive work.

questions.prompt: What does the department consider about an unspent conviction?

options.text: Only the length of the sentence that the court gave to the person
Only the opinion of the candidate's referees about the matter
How serious and old it was, the age at the time, and relevance to the post
Only whether it was the first offence on the person's record

questions.hint: It considers the facts as a whole.

questions.prompt: What is the most damaging thing a candidate can do on the form?

options.text: Declare an unspent conviction on the form even though it is minor
Give a false answer to a question the department may properly ask
Ask what the rules are before you complete the form
Seek advice from an independent adviser about the question

questions.hint: False answers destroy trust.

questions.prompt: Where should an advert say that a post is an excepted one?

options.text: In the payslip of the previous post-holder
In its description or eligibility information
In the induction pack after the offer
In a separate letter sent after the interview

questions.hint: The advert should make this clear.

items.title: Level 4: The life of a right to work check
items.source: Home Office right to work guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: A right to work check is not a single event for everyone. For some workers it is a one-off. A person with an unlimited right to work, such as a British or Irish citizen or someone with settled status, usually needs to be checked only once, at the start. For people whose permission has an end date, the check is a process over time. The employer notes the date, diarises a follow-up check before the date and, if permission is renewed, checks the new evidence. If permission ends and is not renewed, the employer cannot lawfully continue to employ the person in that role, and must take action. Applying to extend permission in time can allow a worker to continue working while the application is decided, but the employer must carry out the correct check to confirm this. Employers may use a manual check of original documents, or an online check where the worker provides a share code. Which method applies depends on the type of status. Some types of status, such as British and Irish passports, can also be checked with approved digital identity technology in some circumstances. Whatever the method, the employer should keep a clear record of what was checked, when and by whom. As an employee, you help by keeping your documents safe, applying to renew on time, and telling your employer of any change. You also help yourself by asking questions early if your status is unclear.

questions.prompt: Who usually needs a right to work check only once?

options.text: People who change employer within the Civil Service after a year
People who have worked for the department for under a year
People with a visa that has an end date
People with an unlimited right to work, such as British or Irish citizens

questions.hint: An unlimited right to work needs checking only at the start.

questions.prompt: What does the employer do for a worker whose permission has an end date?

options.text: Checks only at the end of the first year of the contract
Leaves the date for the worker to track
Notes the date and checks again before it ends
Asks the Home Office to remove the date

questions.hint: A follow-up check is needed before the date.

questions.prompt: What happens if permission ends and is not renewed?

options.text: The employer must pay a fine for each day of delay
The employer must give a 12-month notice period
The employer cannot lawfully keep employing the person in that role
The employer may carry on until the next annual review of staff

questions.hint: Employment without permission is unlawful.

questions.prompt: What can allow a worker to continue working while an extension is decided?

options.text: A note from a previous employer about the worker's status
A letter from the line manager saying the worker may stay on
A promise made by the worker to leave if refused
An application made in time, confirmed by the correct check

questions.hint: The employer must carry out the correct check.

questions.prompt: How may an employer check a worker's right to work?

options.text: By a signed statement from the worker confirming their status
By a manual check of originals or an online check using a share code
By a telephone call to the worker's friends and relatives
By looking at the worker's social media and online profile

questions.hint: These are standard routes.

questions.prompt: What does the choice of check method depend on?

options.text: The type of status the worker has
The worker's clearance level
The worker's salary band
The size of the department

questions.hint: Different statuses have different methods.

questions.prompt: What should the employer record about the check?

options.text: What was checked, when and by whom
The worker's opinion of the process
The worker's hobbies
The names of the worker's referees only

questions.hint: A clear record is part of the duty.

questions.prompt: How can an employee help the process?

options.text: Keep documents safe, apply to renew on time and report changes
Ask a colleague to hold the documents
Avoid mentioning the end date until the day that it falls due
Wait for the employer to ask about status changes at some point

questions.hint: Employees share responsibility.

items.title: Level 4: Why nationality rules exist
items.body: The Civil Service nationality rules are not about the quality or character of any group. They exist because some work needs a particular kind of link to the UK, for example roles dealing with national security, defence or sensitive international matters. The principle is that for the most sensitive work, the government needs to be confident about loyalty and the ability to check a person's background fully. For most jobs the rules are wider. In general, they allow UK nationals, and subject to conditions, citizens of some other countries such as Commonwealth and Irish citizens, and some people who have settled status or other immigration permission. Because these categories can be changed by the government, you should check the current rules when you apply. Different posts have different rules, and a post may be reserved for UK nationals even where the person has the right to work. Dual nationals may be eligible for some reserved posts, but this depends on the post and the other nationality, so do not assume. The nationality rules are separate from security clearance. A person may meet the nationality rule for a post and still need to pass vetting. Equally, someone may be eligible by nationality but not eligible for a role because they have not lived in the UK long enough to be vetted at the level needed. Always read the eligibility statement in the advert, and ask the contact if you are unsure.

questions.prompt: Why do the nationality rules exist?

options.text: To favour people who have worked abroad
To judge the character of different groups of people
Some work needs a particular kind of link to the UK
To reduce the number of applications received

questions.hint: They are linked to the nature of the work.

questions.prompt: What does the government need to be confident about for the most sensitive work?

options.text: Loyalty and being able to check a person's background
The candidate's qualifications and grades
The candidate's political opinions
The candidate's willingness to relocate

questions.hint: Sensitive work needs trust and checkable background.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the rules for most Civil Service jobs?

options.text: They allow only people who were born in the UK itself
They allow only UK nationals in every case and for every job advertised
They are wider and allow some non-UK nationals, with conditions
They allow anyone in the world to apply without conditions

questions.hint: Most jobs are open to more groups than the reserved posts.

questions.prompt: Why should you check the current rules when you apply?

options.text: The rules are changed by each manager
The rules apply only on certain days of the week
The rules differ according to your age
The categories can be changed by the government

questions.hint: Rules can change over time.

questions.prompt: Can a post be reserved for UK nationals even where a person has the right to work?

options.text: Reserved posts apply only in Northern Ireland
Reserved posts can exclude others who have the right to work
Reserved posts apply only to temporary staff
Reserved posts must be open to anyone with the right to work

questions.hint: Reserved posts can exclude people who have the right to work.

questions.prompt: How should dual nationals approach reserved posts?

options.text: Choose which nationality to mention
Check the post's rules rather than assuming eligibility
Assume they are never eligible for reserved posts
Assume they are always eligible for reserved posts

questions.hint: It depends on the post and the other nationality.

questions.prompt: How are the nationality rules related to security clearance?

options.text: They are the same thing, just under two different names
Clearance replaces the nationality rules for all cleared posts
The nationality rules apply only after clearance has been granted
They are separate, and a person may meet one but still need to pass the other

questions.hint: They are separate requirements.

questions.prompt: Why might someone eligible by nationality still not be eligible for a role?

options.text: They live in a different region of the UK from the job
They may not have lived in the UK long enough to be vetted at the level
They are older than the usual age range for this kind of role
They have a different job title from the one advertised

questions.hint: Residence can limit vetting.

items.title: Level 4: Need to know and clearance
items.body: Having security clearance does not give you the right to see everything classified at that level. Government uses a principle called need to know. This means that you should only see or hear sensitive information if you need it to do your job. Clearance shows that you have been assessed as safe to be trusted with material at a certain level, but a separate decision is made about whether you need particular items. A closely related idea is that access should be limited to the minimum necessary. A person with SC clearance who works on benefits correspondence should not browse intelligence reports, even if they could technically find them. Doing so would be a breach of security rules. The reason is simple. The fewer people who know something, the lower the risk of leaks, and the easier it is to find the source if one occurs. Need to know also protects individuals, because no one can be blamed for information they never saw. In practice, you will be given access to the systems and files linked to your role and no more. If you need extra access, ask through your line manager and the proper process. If you are given something by mistake, do not read on out of curiosity. Tell the sender and your security contact. Clearance is a necessary condition for access to sensitive material, but it is never a sufficient one.

questions.prompt: What does need to know mean?

options.text: You should share information with anyone who asks politely and has a pass
You should only see sensitive information if you need it to do your job
You should be told everything held at your clearance level by default
You should keep information only for a limited period

questions.hint: Access depends on the job, not just the clearance.

questions.prompt: What does clearance show?

options.text: That you have been assessed as safe to be trusted with material at a certain level
That you may see any information held at that level of secrecy
That you have a right to promotion to a more senior grade
That you may share information freely with others who also hold clearance

questions.hint: Clearance is permission to be trusted, not a right to see everything.

questions.prompt: Why is browsing reports you do not need a breach, even if you hold the right clearance?

options.text: Cleared people may only read printed documents, not screens
Browsing slows down the computer system
Access should be limited to the minimum necessary for the job
Reports are always protected by a password

questions.hint: Need to know limits access to what the job requires.

questions.prompt: Why does limiting who knows something reduce risk?

options.text: Fewer people know it, so there is less chance of a leak
Information becomes more valuable the more it is shared
It reduces the cost of storing information
More people are available to check the information for errors

questions.hint: Fewer people with access means fewer leak chances.

questions.prompt: How does need to know protect individuals?

options.text: It stops them from ever being asked to give evidence
It guarantees that they will be promoted sooner than others
Nobody can be blamed for information they never saw
It ensures they are paid at the correct rate for the job

questions.hint: It limits the chance of being wrongly implicated.

questions.prompt: What is the right route if you need extra access for your job?

options.text: Ask through your line manager and the proper process
Wait until you are next promoted to a higher grade
Use a colleague's account to get it for the moment
Ask the vetting organisation directly for the extra access

questions.hint: Access is granted through proper channels.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you are given something by mistake?

options.text: Stop reading, and tell the sender and your security contact
Delete it and say nothing to anyone about what you saw
Forward it to a colleague to check what it is
Read it and decide whether it matters to your work

questions.hint: Report it rather than reading further.

questions.prompt: How does clearance relate to access to sensitive material?

options.text: It is required only for printed material
It is necessary but not sufficient
It is sufficient on its own
It has no connection to access

questions.hint: Clearance plus need to know are both required.

items.title: Level 4: How vetting decisions are made
items.body: Vetting is a risk assessment, not a pass or fail test of character. The people doing it ask whether there is a reasonable chance that the person could be a security risk, now or in the future. They look at three broad things. The first is reliability and honesty, shown by how you have behaved in the past and how truthful you are with them. The second is vulnerability to pressure or inducement, for example through serious financial problems, secrets that others could use against you, or close contacts who could put you under pressure. The third is whether there are factors that cast doubt on trustworthiness, such as serious criminal conduct. The question is always about risk in relation to the particular post and its level. The same facts could be acceptable for a lower level and not for a higher one. Decision makers also look at mitigation: what has changed, how recently, and whether risks can be managed. A debt that is being repaid under a plan is very different from one that is ignored. A past mistake that was openly declared is different from one that was hidden. Decisions are expected to be proportionate and consistent, and based on evidence rather than assumption or prejudice. They should not turn on a person's race, religion, sexuality or similar characteristics. If clearance is refused, you can ask for a review and there is an independent route for appeal.

questions.prompt: How is vetting best described?

options.text: A test of knowledge about government
A ranking of candidates by suitability for promotion
A risk assessment, not a pass or fail test of character

options.text: Level of education

Speed of learning
Reliability and honesty

options.text: Being in a hurry to finish the forms before the deadline

Being under pressure from a heavy workload you cannot manage
Being open to pressure, for example through serious money problems

questions.hint: Vulnerability relates to others exploiting a weakness.

options.text: The vetting team changes its rules each week as it chooses
Lower levels are not checked at all
The risk is judged in relation to the post and its level
Higher levels are decided by different people with other powers

questions.hint: Risk is related to what the post gives access to.

questions.prompt: What does mitigation mean in this context?

options.text: What has changed and whether risks can be managed
A delay while more checks are done on the person
A penalty that is added to the clearance decision
A reduction in the clearance level that is awarded

questions.hint: Mitigation reduces the level of risk.

questions.prompt: How is a debt under a repayment plan viewed compared with one that is ignored?

options.text: It is treated more seriously, as it shows planning ahead
It is very different, because the person is dealing with it
It is not considered by the vetting team
It is treated the same, as only the amount of debt matters

questions.hint: Management of a problem is a positive sign.

options.text: The impression made at interview
The number of questions the candidate asked in the interview
Evidence rather than assumption or prejudice
The reputation of the candidate's referees at work

questions.hint: Decisions must be fair and proportionate.

options.text: Ask your referees to resubmit the form
Apply for a different clearance level immediately afterwards
Nothing, as the decision is final
Ask for a review, and there is an independent appeal route

questions.hint: Review and appeal routes exist.

items.title: Level 4: Living abroad and residence
items.body: Time spent living outside the UK is common and is not a bar to joining the Civil Service. It matters mainly for security clearance, and in general the higher the level, the more it matters. The reason is practical. Vetting relies on records and on people who can speak about you. If you have lived in the UK for a long time, there are many records, such as addresses, employers, banks and referees, that can be checked. If you have spent long periods abroad, the vetting team may have fewer checkable records, and checks overseas can be harder or impossible. For this reason, clearance levels usually expect a minimum period of UK residence, and the advert will say if one applies. The period is longer for higher levels, but the exact figure depends on the role and can change, so use the advert rather than assuming. A shorter residence history does not always mean refusal. The vetting team can sometimes use other checks, and in some cases the department may be willing to wait until the person has been resident for longer. If you have lived abroad, list the countries and dates carefully and be ready to give contacts who can confirm your time there. For the baseline, time abroad is treated as part of your employment history and does not by itself cause a problem. If you are unsure whether your history will meet a role's requirement, ask the contact in the advert before you apply.

questions.prompt: How does living outside the UK affect joining the Civil Service?

options.text: It is a bar, but only for managers and senior staff
It never matters for any check at any level
It is not a bar, but it can matter for clearance
It is a bar in every case and for every role

questions.hint: Time abroad is common and matters mainly for security clearance.

questions.prompt: Why does time abroad matter more at higher clearance levels?

options.text: Higher levels only accept people who were born in the UK itself, no exceptions
Time abroad is treated as a conviction at the higher levels
Vetting relies on records and people, which are harder to check abroad
Higher levels are decided by a different country's officials

questions.hint: Fewer checkable records make vetting harder.

questions.prompt: What do clearance levels usually expect?

options.text: A minimum period of UK residence
A minimum number of foreign languages
A minimum number of jobs held
A minimum number of references

questions.hint: Residence helps the vetting team check your background.

options.text: In the induction pack
In the contract of a colleague
On the vetting organisation's noticeboard
In the advert

questions.hint: The advert states any requirement.

options.text: The figure is fixed by law and never changes over time
The figure is the same for every role
The figure depends on the role and can change

questions.hint: The requirement varies and can change over time.

options.text: It always means refusal, with no exceptions at all

Other checks may be possible, or the department may wait

questions.hint: Flexibility sometimes exists.

questions.hint: Detailed accounts help vetting.

options.text: As a conviction that must be declared on the criminal record form
As a reason to be cleared at a higher level than the job needs
As part of your employment history, not a problem by itself
As a gap that cannot be explained or put right

questions.hint: For the BPSS, it forms part of your history.

items.title: Level 4: Aftercare and changes of circumstance
items.body: Getting clearance is not the end of the process. Security is about managing risk over time, because people's lives change. This is called aftercare. It means that the department and the individual keep the information up to date and watch for changes that could affect the risk. As a cleared person you are expected to report significant changes. Typical examples include a new partner or close contact, a change in finances such as serious debt, a criminal charge or conviction, and changes in nationality or residence. You should also report anything that makes you feel under pressure from others, or any approach that seems suspicious. Reporting a change does not mean you will lose your clearance. In most cases the security team can note it and agree a way forward. The greater risk is not reporting. Clearance is reviewed at intervals, and the length of time between reviews is longer for lower levels and shorter for higher levels. At a review you may complete an updated questionnaire. If you move to another job in the Civil Service, your clearance can often be transferred, provided it is still in date, it is at the right level for the new role, and the new sponsor requests it. If it has lapsed or is too low, the new employer must request fresh vetting. Managers also have a part: they should notice and report changes in behaviour that could be a concern, and they should support the person while this happens.

questions.prompt: What is meant by aftercare for someone who holds clearance?

options.text: A welfare scheme for staff who are ill for a long period or on leave
Keeping clearance information up to date and watching for changes in risk
A review of how well the induction went for new staff in the first month
A refund of travel and hotel expenses after a security interview with UKSV

questions.hint: Aftercare manages risk over time.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical change to report if you hold clearance?

A change of mobile phone model or network provider that you use

options.text: Your clearance ends immediately in every case

options.text: Reporting a change in writing

Not reporting a change

options.text: Reviews are the same for every level

items.title: Level 4: The Official Secrets Act and confidentiality
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Civil servants are given access to information that members of the public do not see, and the law and the Civil Service Code set rules on how it is used. The Official Secrets Act 1989 makes it a criminal offence for certain people, including civil servants and government contractors, to disclose protected information without lawful authority. The protected categories include security and intelligence, defence, international relations and information that would help criminals. Not every piece of government information is covered by the Act. Most of your work is OFFICIAL, and misuse of it can be dealt with under other laws and under disciplinary rules. In practice you will usually be briefed on the Act at the start of a job, and some departments ask staff to sign a declaration to show they understand. The duty of confidentiality does not end when you leave. You must not disclose protected information after you have left the Civil Service. There are lawful routes to raise concerns or to disclose information when authorised, such as using the departmental whistleblowing process or the Civil Service Commission. The Act is not meant to stop honest reporting of wrongdoing through proper channels. Alongside the Act, data protection law and the Civil Service Code require care with personal information. If you are unsure whether something may be shared, ask your line manager or the security team before you act, not afterwards.

questions.prompt: What does the Official Secrets Act 1989 do?

options.text: Makes it an offence for some people to disclose protected information
Sets the pay and grade of civil servants who handle secret material
Gives civil servants the right to publish any information they hold
Requires all government information to be published every year by law

questions.hint: It criminalises unauthorised disclosure of protected information.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a category of information protected by the Act?

options.text: Staff canteen menus and opening hours
Public holiday dates for the year
Office furniture orders for the building
Security and intelligence

questions.hint: Security, defence and international relations are covered.

options.text: It covers information that comes from abroad, but not UK information
It covers paper documents only, and not electronic files or emails
It covers every document and email held by a department of government
It covers set categories, and most OFFICIAL material falls under other rules

questions.hint: The Act covers defined categories only.

questions.prompt: When are you usually told about the Official Secrets Act?

options.text: After your first disciplinary meeting, if one is ever held with your manager
At the start of a job, in a briefing, sometimes with a signed declaration
When you leave the Civil Service, at the end of your final day
At your first annual review with your line manager, a year in

questions.hint: New starters are briefed early.

questions.prompt: How long does the duty of confidentiality under the Act last?

options.text: It ends after one year of leaving
It continues after you leave the Civil Service
It continues after you leave, but applies only to managers
It ends on the last day of the job

questions.hint: The duty continues.

questions.prompt: Which is a lawful route for raising a concern?

options.text: The departmental whistleblowing process or the Civil Service Commission
A message to a journalist who covers government news
A message to a friend outside work who works in a newspaper
A public social media post naming the people involved

questions.hint: Proper channels protect both the person and the information.

questions.prompt: What is the Act not meant to prevent?

options.text: Publication of official statistics by a government department
Use of work email for ordinary day-to-day messages between staff
Staff discussing information that is already in the public domain
Honest reporting of wrongdoing through proper channels

questions.hint: Proper reporting is protected.

options.text: After you have shared it, if asked
Only when it is marked TOP SECRET
Only when it concerns another department
Before you act, not afterwards

questions.hint: Asking first avoids breaches.

items.title: Level 4: Fairness, equality and adjustments in checks
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination in employment, including in recruitment and pre-employment checks. The protected characteristics are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. The Civil Service is expected to set an example, and checks and vetting must be applied fairly. They should be about security risk and legal requirements, not about who a person is. For example, someone's religion or sexuality should not be a reason for refusing clearance. What can be considered is actual behaviour or circumstances that create risk, such as being open to pressure because of a secret. Employers must also make reasonable adjustments for disabled applicants and staff. This can apply during recruitment and checks as well as in the job, for example allowing more time to complete a form, providing documents in an accessible format, or arranging an interview in a suitable place. You do not have to give detailed medical information. Usually you just need to explain what would help. The Civil Service also runs the Disability Confident scheme and the Guaranteed Interview Scheme, which offers an interview to disabled applicants who meet the minimum criteria. If you need an adjustment, ask the recruitment contact as early as you can. Information you give about your health is treated as confidential and is used only for the purpose for which it was given.

options.text: The Official Secrets Act 1989

The Data Protection Act 2018

A person's religion or other beliefs held privately

questions.hint: Actual risk factors can be considered, not characteristics.

items.title: Level 4: Reporting, learning and probation
items.body: In your first months you are expected to learn, to follow the rules and to speak up when something goes wrong. Departments treat mandatory learning as part of your probation, and managers may check that it has been done. Beyond the courses, you should build good working habits: keep your objectives in mind, record what you do, ask for feedback and use one-to-ones to raise issues early. When a mistake happens, the expected response is to report it promptly. This applies to security incidents, such as losing a pass, to data incidents, such as sending a message to the wrong person, and to any other error that could cause harm. Departments run learning cultures in which people are encouraged to report so lessons can be shared, but deliberate breaches and cover-ups can lead to disciplinary action. If you have a concern about wrongdoing, such as fraud, bullying or a breach of the Civil Service Code, you can raise it with your line manager, a senior colleague, a nominated officer or through the department's confidential route. If you are not satisfied, you can take it to the Civil Service Commission. You are protected for honest reporting. Probation is also the time to say if you need support, for example reasonable adjustments, a different training format or a buddy. A good new starter is not someone who never makes a mistake. It is someone who learns, asks and tells people when something is wrong.
